title: Offline: my year without a smartphone
text: Last January I made a decision that my friends considered either brave or ridiculous: I swapped my smartphone for an old phone that can only make calls and send text messages. It was not a New Year's resolution, exactly. Rather, it was the result of a bad week in December, when I realised that I was spending more than six hours a day staring at a screen and could not remember a single thing I had watched. I told nobody about the plan, in case I failed within a week.

The first days were harder than I expected. I kept reaching into my pocket to check the weather, the time, the news, anything at all, and finding nothing there. On the bus, where everyone else was looking down at a glowing rectangle, I felt as if I had been left out of a secret. I also discovered how much I depended on the phone for small tasks. Without a map, I got lost twice in a city where I had lived for five years, and I was late to a friend's birthday party because I could not check the timetable. A taxi driver, seeing my old phone, asked whether I was making a film about the past.

Slowly, however, things changed. I began to read again, first on the bus and then before bed, and by March I had finished eleven books. I noticed details I had never paid attention to: a small bakery on my street, the colour of the evening sky, the way my neighbour whistles when he waters his plants. My friends, who at first teased me, started to phone me instead of writing, and our conversations became longer and more interesting. My grandmother, who has never learnt to text, was delighted. I even began to cook proper meals, because I no longer ate with one eye on a screen.

Not everything improved. Group chats continued without me, and more than once I learnt about a plan only after it had already happened. A classmate admitted that she had stopped inviting me to things because she assumed I would not see the message. That hurt, and it made me wonder whether my experiment was an act of independence or simply a way of avoiding people. In the end I decided it was neither. It was an experiment, and like all experiments, it showed me something I had not predicted.

By the summer I had stopped counting the days. I still used a computer for homework, and I admit that I sometimes borrowed my brother's phone when I needed a taxi or a ticket. Strictly speaking, that was cheating, and my brother never let me forget it. But the habit of checking constantly had gone. I could sit in a café for an hour without feeling nervous about what I might be missing, which seemed to me the greatest achievement of the whole year. My marks at school did not change much, although my teachers said I seemed calmer.

In December I bought a new smartphone, but I use it differently now. Notifications are switched off, and the phone stays in my bag during meals. I do not recommend my experiment to everyone: it would be impossible for people whose work depends on being reachable. Yet I would suggest a smaller version of it, a day or two a month, to anybody who suspects that their screen has more influence on their life than they would like to admit. My little sister has already asked to try it, but I told her to wait until she is older.

questions.q: What made the author decide to change his phone?
options: He had lost his smartphone just before New Year.
He wanted to follow a New Year tradition.
He was shocked by the way he spent his time.
A friend had dared him to do it.

questions.q: How did the author feel on the bus in the first days?
options: Relieved to be free of constant distractions at last.
Angry with the people around him.
Worried about being robbed.
Excluded from what the others were doing.

questions.q: Which problem is NOT mentioned in paragraph 2?
options: Having trouble paying for a bus ticket.
Losing his way twice in a familiar city.
Arriving late at a party.
Being unable to check the time.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, what does 'That' in 'That hurt' refer to?
options: Finding out about a plan after it had happened.
Learning that a classmate no longer invited him.
Losing contact with his grandmother.
Hearing his friends criticise the experiment openly.

questions.q: What does the author mean by 'I had stopped counting the days' in paragraph 5?
options: He had lost interest in the project.
The summer holidays had begun.
He had completed the experiment.
He no longer felt it as a struggle.

questions.q: What does the author consider his greatest achievement?
options: Feeling calm without checking a phone.
Reading eleven books by the spring.
Staying completely offline for a year.
Persuading friends to phone him.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude to his experiment in the last paragraph?
options: He thinks everybody should repeat it.
He regrets returning to a smartphone.
He finds it useful but not suitable for all.
He believes smartphones should be banned for children.

discuss: Could you live without a smartphone for a week? What would be the hardest part?
The author says screens can influence our lives more than we admit. Do you agree?
What rules about phone use would you introduce in your family or class?
